title: Jevolution: A Framework for Studying Communication and Collective Dynamics in AI Agents
comment: 29 pages, 5 figures, 12 tables. Project website: https://jevolution.world
summary: Experiments with remote decision-making agents depend on more than the policy: the world may change during inference, the simulator determines which actions are available, and births and immigration alter who can act. We present Jevolution, an instrumented spatial predator-prey framework that makes these dependencies explicit. Its reference implementation separates the evolving world, asynchronous request scheduling, controller adapters, and experiment records. The model combines local observations, energy and resource constraints, predefined signals, and inherited scalar traits. We describe these mechanisms using the ODD protocol and distinguish implemented controls from research questions requiring additional interventions. Free synthetic fixtures exercise scheduling, signaling, and inheritance against the pinned implementation; they validate specified software behavior rather than model intelligence or ecological realism. A completed communication case study illustrates the end-to-end workflow using Jev to control both species. Across 6 complete habitat-seed pairs, the mean signals-on minus signals-off difference in normalized rabbit abundance was -0.0095 (nominal 95% pair-bootstrap interval [-0.0772, 0.0602]). This small study does not resolve the direction of the signal-system effect. The contribution is an inspectable experimental system and its evidence boundaries, not a new policy-learning algorithm or a demonstration of emergent language, adaptive selection, or biological predictive validity.

title: Optimize Once, Execute Fast: Latency-Aware Multi-Agent Workflow Learning for Recurrent Queries
summary: Large Language Model-based Multi-Agent Systems (LLM-based MAS) have shown remarkable success in solving complex tasks by coordinating specialized agents through multi-step workflows. To overcome the high cost and specificity of manually designed workflows, recent research has shifted toward learning them automatically. However, a key limitation remains: while agent calls introduce significant latency due to model inference time and service congestion, most automated methods optimize solely for downstream performance, ignoring execution time (makespan). This issue is amplified when workflows are reused across recurring queries, making latency accumulate over time. This limits deployment in recurrent applications such as AI customer support and AI cloud troubleshooting, where users expect fast responses. To bridge this gap, we introduce a new problem, termed latency-aware workflow generation, where the objective is to minimize workflow makespan while aiming to retain downstream performance. We propose LAWA (Latency-Aware Workflow optimizAtion), a novel framework that reduces makespan via theoretically grounded graph edits targeting critical-path bottlenecks. By unifying a graph generator with this graph-editing procedure, LAWA supports both de novo workflow generation and refinement of existing ones. Empirical results across seven benchmarks demonstrate that LAWA significantly reduces makespan while achieving competitive task performance, supporting efficient reuse of multi-agent workflows for recurrent queries.

title: SEPM: Self-Evolving Procedural Memory Grounded in Task Graphs for Multi-Agent Collaboration
summary: Long-horizon multi-agent collaboration requires memory that preserves both successful actions and the coordination structure underlying them. Existing memory systems support information sharing or procedural reuse, but often leave the evolution of shared procedures disconnected from the task dependencies and execution states of collaborating agents. This coupling also limits the direct transfer of procedural memory designed for individual agents to team settings. We propose Self-Evolving Procedural Memory (SEPM), a framework that uses task dependency graphs as a common representation for online coordination and procedural memory evolution. During execution, a lightweight shared blackboard records structured evidence alongside task dependencies, supporting the detection of goal, plan, and world-state divergence and evidence-based realignment. After execution, verified actions and dependencies are distilled into reusable procedures, while recurring failures inform warnings and constraints. The shared procedure pool evolves through creation, refinement, specialization, and retirement, guided by success and cost utility and constrained by evidence and safety requirements. Together, these mechanisms preserve the collaborative structure and applicability conditions needed to reuse experience across tasks. Evaluations on ALFWorld, WebArena, and OfficeBench under AutoGen and DyLAN show that SEPM achieves the highest task scores among the compared methods in all six benchmark settings. Under AutoGen, it improves task scores over the no-added-memory baseline by 29.85, 25.86, and 13.00 percentage points, respectively. The codebase is available at https://github.com/cookieApril/SEPM.

title: sGLP: Specifying Stochastic Agents that Simulate People
summary:
Grassroots platforms are designed to be owned, operated and governed by their participants, and thus are constituted from person-to-person smartphone apps that run on participants' smartphones. A grassroots app is specified using a grassroots social contract, which is compiled through an abstraction cascade into a volition-guarded Grassroots Logic Program (vGLP), a multiagent concurrent logic programming language. A vGLP program in turn specifies a smartphone UI via which people express their volitions and thus control the app. Prudence dictates large-scale evaluation and testing of grassroots platforms prior to deployment, but using the many people needed to do that is a contradiction in terms. Hence another solution is needed.
  Here, we present stochastic GLP (sGLP), designed to allow grassroots platforms to be simulated at scale from the vGLP programs that deploy them, with stochastic agents in place of people. sGLP is GLP with a rate extension for specifying stochastic behaviour. A stochastic agent is an sGLP program replacing both the vGLP UI and the person behind it. It is typed by the dual of the interactive type of the UI and specifies a stochastic profile of a person's behaviour.
  We demonstrate sGLP on the grassroots social graph, with a population of men and women drawn from four stochastic profiles --- homophile or indifferent, wary or sociable --- and on grassroots currencies, with four profiles --- spenders or savers, cautious or generous --- and report what the mix of profiles does to the social graph that forms and to the currencies that circulate.
  We prove that every run of a vGLP program in which sGLP agents replace the UI and the people behind it is a vGLP run. We implemented sGLP in GLP by Gillespie's method, and ran reproducible simulations with it.

title: MDN-VJEPA: Multimodal Probabilistic Joint-Embedding World Models
summary: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) learn world models by predicting future representations rather than reconstructing observations. Variational JEPA (VJEPA) gives this prediction probabilistic semantics and permits flexible conditional predictive families. We propose MDN-VJEPA, a multimodal probabilistic JEPA that instantiates the latent predictor as a mixture density network (MDN), representing future states with a Gaussian mixture whose components encode alternative futures, their probabilities, and within-mode uncertainty. For sequential prediction, we address two additional structural requirements: multi-modal futures should remain temporally coherent across a trajectory, and predictive beliefs should remain consistent when propagated to the same horizon through different temporal path compositions, as motivated by the Chapman--Kolmogorov equation. Together, these considerations define a three-level hierarchy of multimodal prediction, coherent multimodal trajectories, and compositionally consistent multimodal dynamics. Controlled experiments show that MDN-VJEPA closely recovers known branching predictive laws, that retaining the complete multimodal belief rather than its conditional mean can lead to materially different and substantially better planning decisions under branching futures, and that trajectory-level coupling and distributional consistency improve temporal coherence and multi-horizon agreement. These results support a simple principle: a probabilistic JEPA should preserve not only how uncertain the future is, but which distinct futures constitute that uncertainty, how they form coherent trajectories, and how those beliefs compose through time.

title: Artificiality's First Exam: An LLM-Referenced C-test for Supraintelligence
comment: Preprint, under review. 63 pages. Code and data at https://github.com/jorallo/ctest-one
summary: Under the accelerated pace of AI development, any benchmark whose difficulty is calibrated with humans or current AI systems becomes circular, or saturates soon. How can we then evaluate machines that may become more capable than the current machines and the people who write the tests? One answer to the question hinges on inverse problems, inductive inference questions for which difficulty depends on the complexity of the underlying mechanism, given the observations and the previous knowledge. Levin's Kt, a computable variant of Kolmogorov complexity, puts a theoretical upper bound to that difficulty, balancing the simplest representation encoding for the mechanism and the logarithm of the time steps to run that mechanism. Previous tests derived from Levin's Kt, such as the original C-test, are based on minimalistic Universal Turing Machines (UTM), capable of very limited representations and no previous knowledge. Reasoning large language models (LLM) are UTMs that capture a compendium of human culture as knowledge, using prompts as natural language programs. This paper presents the first test based on Levin's Kt with LLMs as representational machines. Fresh test items can be produced at high difficulties, estimated in a ratio scale measured in bits, before any human or frontier model can solve them. We formalise the measure, devise a lightweight generation and certification pipeline, explore the effect of the power of the reference machine and the gap between examiner and examinee. We produce a first battery of certified items administered to twelve LLMs. The resulting agent characteristic curves decrease with difficulty, down to the uncharted high-difficulty region, the supra-intelligence window of items we can certify, yet beyond generations of frontier intelligence.

title: EAIR: Interaction Risks in Enterprise LLM Multi-Agent Systems
summary: LLM agents increasingly divide enterprise work across roles with different goals, authority, access, and information. Because each agent often sees only a local snapshot of the enterprise workflow, locally reasonable actions can still violate organization-wide constraints (e.g., several service agents can each issue credit that is individually permitted while collectively exceeding a shared compensation cap). We introduce EAIR, the first framework for analyzing enterprise multi-agent interaction risks. We make four contributions. (1) We formalize enterprise interaction risk in terms of the organizational properties that workflow operations must preserve, and operationalize this formulation as a taxonomy of testable risks with explicit failure criteria and evidence requirements. (2) We build EAIR-Worlds, a suite of executable micro-worlds that instantiates selected risks as controlled, observable workflows with explicit roles, policies, permissions, source facts, and execution traces. (3) We develop a novel diagnosis-and-repair pipeline that uses the resulting execution traces to locate contributing interaction boundaries, guide targeted workflow repairs, and retest the repaired system. (4) Large-scale experiments show recurring interaction failures across the organizational properties studied. Together, EAIR is the first operational framework for diagnosing and mitigating enterprise multi-agent interaction failures.

title: LACRM: LLM-Guided Mining of Directed Advertiser Competition Relationships in E-Commerce Advertising
summary: In e-commerce advertising, ad platforms typically fail to model the externalities among advertisers when making optimization decisions: an advertiser's actual performance is largely shaped by rivals competing for the same users; these rivals typically operate in overlapping product categories and at comparable budget scales. However, capturing this rivalry as an explicit, reusable signal is challenging because it is directed, multi-faceted, and partially observable. Existing paradigms such as interaction graphs, taxonomy rules, and single-embedding models do not fully capture these properties. In this paper, we propose LACRM (LLM-driven Advertiser Competition Relationship Mining), a novel framework that constructs directed competition graphs with continuous edge intensities via a three-stage pipeline. LACRM moves beyond symmetric similarity through LLM-driven role-separated profiling, which enables asymmetric multi-route retrieval to uncover both realized and latent rivals. The framework further incorporates listwise learning-to-rank aligned with temporal auction behavior to accurately model directed competition intensity. In offline retrieval experiments on an industrial benchmark, LACRM outperforms strong directed GNN baselines and ablation variants. Multi-LLM and human studies provide complementary evidence that the recovered latent rivals reflect meaningful market competition rather than merely model-generated artifacts. In production A/B tests, LACRM-guided bidding and incentive allocation increase advertising revenue by 1.73% and 1.14%, respectively. The results demonstrate the practical value of explicit competition modeling in large-scale advertising systems.

title: The Silent Failures in Agentic Data Science
summary: Large language models have significantly lowered the barrier to writing code. Naturally, this has also led to the development of data science agents that promise automating the design and execution of data science from task formulation to model development. Existing evaluations of agentic data science (agentic DS) assess downstream predictive performance and code correctness, providing preliminary insight in agentic DS capabilities. We argue that these evaluations overlook the fundamental principles of data science: methodological data science- and domain knowledge. As such, only assessing downstream performance masks methodological failures such as data leakage and inappropriate validation, limiting the development of robust agentic DS systems. In this paper, we evaluate agentic DS beyond accuracy from three different angles: 1) a large-scale analysis of failure modes in common agentic DS frameworks and models across 220 data science tasks, 2) a reusable and extensible test suite with curated data science tasks that test for six specific failures in a controlled manner, and 3) a qualitative assessment of agentic DS pipelines against expert solutions on Kaggle competitions. We find that the majority of agentic solutions contain at least one failure mode despite the complexity of agentic harness or model capacity. Moreover, we identify a positive correlation between the occurrence of data leakage failures and predictive performance, confirming the necessity to evaluate agents beyond accuracy. Our qualitative analysis shows that DS agents generally lack problem solving creativity and domain knowledge, compared to competition-winning data scientists. We believe that principled failure mode analysis, as presented here, should be integral part of agentic DS evaluations, and that the insights we surface will be key in developing trustworthy agentic DS pipelines.

title: Persistent LLM Orchestration of Heterogeneous Robot Teams via Partial Delegation to Multi-Agent Protocols
summary: Natural language specifications let non-expert users task robot teams, and large language models (LLMs) have recently proven effective at grounding such semantic specifications into plans for heterogeneous teams. Existing approaches assume missions that terminate and environments that, while unknown, do not change, but both assumptions fail in many emerging applications. For example, a disaster-response mission does not terminate, and its environment changes continuously as hazards spread and evacuees move. We identify three ways an LLM orchestrator breaks in this setting: its prompt grows without bound, its reasoning degrades as agents and targets accumulate, and it stops actively monitoring after covering the search space once. We build on the successful framework of grounded generative intelligence, and address each issue with a classical idea. A Markovian state summary, rebuilt from the semantic map at every invocation, replaces the growing interaction history. Partial delegation lets the orchestrator assign a subset of robots to an autonomous multi-agent protocol and reserve its reasoning for generating subtasks that require detailed parameters and careful ordering. Lastly, observation staleness, surfaced explicitly in the prompt, together with task-and event-triggered re-prompting, keeps the team vigilant. In a simulated urban search-and-rescue mission with spreading fire and moving evacuees, our framework rescues 98% of civilians versus 89% for the strongest baseline while using six times fewer tokens. Additional ablations isolate the contribution of each mechanism.

title: MRFlow: Mechanism-Structured Residual Flow Matching for Virtual Cell Perturbation Prediction
summary: Predicting cellular responses to chemical and genetic perturbations is a central test for AI virtual cells, yet many single-cell models reduce each condition to an average expression shift. This target is misaligned with perturbation biology: rare states, resistant subpopulations, and context-dependent effect sizes may coexist under the same intervention. MRFlow treats virtual-cell prediction as conditional transport between empirical single-cell measures. Control and perturbed cells are embedded in a variational latent state space, greedy low-cost supervision is constructed over detached minibatch states, and a conditional flow-matching vector field transports control populations toward perturbed populations. The field decomposes into a mechanism-structured affine dictionary, which recombines shared latent response operators with a low-rank condition-specific correction, and a spectrally controlled residual field for nonlinear cell-level variation. Genetic perturbations are encoded through a regulatory-graph GCN, chemical perturbations through Morgan fingerprints, and both enter the same conditional dynamics interface. Across eight gene and drug perturbation benchmarks, MRFlow attains the highest composite score while preserving competitive raw performance on differential-expression and distributional metrics. The results support latent distribution transport as a principled and empirically effective formulation for perturbation-aware virtual cell modeling.

title: ClawLoop: Self-Improving Agents via Harness-Native Training Loop
summary: The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has driven their deployment toward general-purpose harness environments, where LLM-based agents operate in sandbox workspaces and interact directly with file systems and shells. While numerous post-training pipelines exist for tool-use agents, their counterparts for harness-based agents remain scarce and are predominantly one-shot and teacher-dependent: a stronger external model synthesizes tasks and collects trajectories, the target agent is trained once, and evaluation results are consumed by human researchers rather than fed back into the loop. Such pipelines are inherently bounded by the capability of the external model and the scope of human prior, leaving no room for self-improvement. To address these limitations, we propose ClawLoop, a framework that enables self-improving without any external teacher model and with minimal prior dependencies. ClawLoop composes three phases into a self-sustaining cycle: Task Synthesis, which generates a diverse pool of training tasks via two complementary construction routines, applies diagnosis-conditioned difficulty growth followed by both agent-free and agent-based task validation; Training, which updates the agent via SFT and/or RL; and Diagnosis and Feedback, which analyzes the agent's rollout behaviors to produce a capability analysis report that will be used as feedback for task synthesis in the next iteration. Using Qwen3.6-27B as the loop model, ClawLoop yields consistent improvements on SkillsBench, Claw-Eval-Live, and ClawGym-Bench. The iteratively refined tasks are further transferred to smaller-scale Qwen3.5-4B and 9B models with gains across all benchmarks, validating data quality independently of the loop model.

title: Do Rollups Self-Organize? Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning in the EIP-4844 Blob Fee Market
comment: 5 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the 2026 IEEE 4th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Blockchain, and Internet of Things (AIBThings 2026)
summary: EIP-4844 gave Ethereum rollups a separate fee dimension for data, governed by a multiplicative update rule that targets three ``blobs'' per block. Whether this target is reached depends on how many independent, self-interested rollups choose to post data, a question that closed-form models address only for a single agent under exogenous prices or in a static equilibrium. We propose a calibrated multi-agent reinforcement learning environment for the blob fee market in which the blob base fee is endogenous, set by the EIP-4844 rule on the aggregated decisions of heterogeneous rollups fit to post-Dencun Ethereum data. After confirming that the environment reproduces the known single-agent analytical optimum, we show that independent learners, with no convergence guarantee, still settle near the target without coordination ($3.32\pm0.01$ blobs per block over five seeds). Over a fiftyfold demand range ($10\times$ to $500\times$), supply stays at the target from $10\times$ to $200\times$ and rises above it at higher demand, where the fee can no longer hold it. Posting frequency increases with rollup size, an emergent analog of the size threshold predicted by prior theory. A costless layer-1 calldata outside option pushes the fee down by roughly an order of magnitude while aggregate supply stays at the target, so the fee rule acts as a negative-feedback controller on decentralized supply.

title: PRIME: Frequency-Aware Unified Pruning and Merging for MoE Compression
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have emerged as an effective paradigm for scaling large language models, yet their massive parameter footprint poses severe memory challenges for deployment. Existing compression methods typically treat expert pruning and merging as disjoint operations and rely on greedy heuristics, often leading to irreversible information loss or representational pollution. In this paper, we propose PRIME, a unified optimization framework for MoE compression via adaptive PRunIng and MErging. PRIME casts the discrete prune-merge assignment step as a global Integer Linear Programming over a frequency-weighted surrogate objective, jointly selecting pruning and merging decisions while accounting for expert usage. We motivate the frequency-aware objective through an error-bound analysis under fixed representative assignments, and show that the formulation favors high-frequency experts as centroids, promoting routing stability. Extensive experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B demonstrate that PRIME achieves strong accuracy retention across knowledge, coding, math, and long-context tasks, while serving benchmarks of merged models quantify the memory and throughput benefits of expert compression in vLLM.

title: Correction Training for Diffusion Models
summary: Iterative sampling in diffusion models can lead to error accumulation due to exposure bias. The denoiser is trained on real images interpolated with noise, but at inference its inputs are constructed from its own imperfect predictions from the earlier steps, something it has never seen at training time. This might be one reason diffusion models often struggle without additional help, such as CFG. We introduce a correction step for diffusion models which attempts to reduce this training-inference gap. The corrector takes the base model's prediction as input and is trained against the same ground-truth target. This makes correction an explicit learning task, with training inputs provided by the base model. During sampling, at each denoising step, we iteratively refine the denoiser's clean-sample prediction. This allows us to correct predictions at intermediate denoising steps, preventing early artifacts from persisting into the final sample. Although the corrector is trained only on predictions from the base denoiser, it can be applied repeatedly to its own outputs at inference for better results. This simple framework leads to substantial improvement in sample quality while largely preserving diversity. We evaluate our method across DiT, SiT, and JiT. Our method substantially improves upon previously reported FID scores for unguided generation and, notably, unconditional generation, where producing high-quality samples without guidance has been particularly challenging. Our method achieves performance competitive with classifier-free guidance (CFG), and combining correction with CFG further improves diversity and reduces oversaturation typical of CFG. Finally, we show that the additional inference cost of correction can be amortized by distilling the refined predictions back into the base diffusion model, retaining the quality gains without additional inference-time overhead.

title: Dynamic Conflict Clustering with Lightweight Learning and Strategic Repair for Distributed Constraint Satisfaction
summary: Distributed Constraint Satisfaction Problems (DCSPs) model distributed decision-making in multi-agent systems, where agents assign values to local variables while satisfying shared constraints. However, many DCSP solvers still rely on broad, repeated peer-to-peer communication and are largely reactive, with limited support for strategic coordination or learning. This increases communication overhead, can lead to stagnation, and reduces the success of hard instances. Hence, we propose Dynamic Conflict Clustering-Incomplete (DCC-Incomplete), a repair-based solver that combines conflict-centred decomposition, structured coordination, strategic repair, and lightweight learning for stagnation recovery. DCC-Incomplete groups the unsolved part of the problem into conflict clusters and restricts communication via a coordination layer to agents within the same conflict region. It also introduces memory-guided restart, enabling agents and clusters to pause, revise, and adapt repairs based on neighbouring conflict states. A thorough evaluation of DCC-Incomplete on distributed graph-colouring benchmarks with planted satisfying assignments shows that its memory-guided restart improves the success rate from 37.50% to 61.11%, reduces median runtime from 0.565s to 0.367s, and cuts median communication from 12.493 to 6.503 messages per constraint. These results suggest that dynamic conflict clustering, combined with lightweight strategic and learning-guided repair, improves both communication efficiency and robustness in incomplete DCSP solving.

title: DoSA: Dots Sparse Attention
summary: Sparse attention visits few keys, yet finding them can still require scoring every key with every indexer head. We introduce DoSA (Dots Sparse Attention), a lossless method for making this computation conditional while preserving exact token selection. Its central observation is that Top-K selection requires sufficient evidence to reject a candidate, not necessarily its full score. A seed set supplies a lower bound on the winning threshold. Nonnegative head projections and joint residual bounds upper-bound positive contributions, while activation-informed aggregation bounds the magnitude subtracted by negative heads. The certificate directs full scoring toward candidates that remain eligible; exact-score filtering further reduces writeback and selection work. We establish the certificate and its exact-selection conditions, and analyze how geometry and selection margins govern its effectiveness. Our GPU implementation accelerates the complete Indexer by up to 2.74 times over SGLang and 1.69 times over LiteTopK across English, Chinese, and code workloads. End-to-end evaluation on GLM-5.2 and DeepSeek-V3.2 achieves up to 1.94 times and 1.50 times time-to-first-token speedups over the two baselines, respectively.

title: Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench 2.0: Automating Diverse Task Construction and Measuring Sustained Agent Progress
summary: Long-horizon terminal benchmarks measure whether an agent can sustain progress through extended workflows with process rewards, not only whether its final state passes a binary check. We present Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench 2.0 (LHTB 2.0), an extension of Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench that preserves its 46 original tasks while correcting task and evaluation-infrastructure defects and extending 31 tasks. LHTB 2.0 contains 77 tasks across 13 domains and eight task types. The extended tasks are produced through a systematic reconstruction-task pipeline. We start from a working scientific or engineering artifact, then use a parameterized reference implementation to generate multiple scenarios, reveal six as behavioral evidence, hold out three for evaluation, and use dense progress ladders to reward partial progress while preventing memorization of public outputs. We also extend the evaluation horizon from 90 minutes to three hours and record verifier checkpoints every 30 minutes, enabling direct measurement of sustained progress within a run. Across 1,145 scored model-task runs from 15 frontier models, GPT-6-astra leads with dense mean reward 0.69 and 37 tasks at R at least 0.95, followed by GPT-5.6-sol with dense mean reward 0.67 and 32 tasks at the same threshold. On the 30 reconstruction tasks, binary verifier scores average 0.221, whereas dense ladder scores average 0.653, showing that outcome-only evaluation discards substantial intermediate progress. LHTB 2.0 provides a broader, hardened, and process-aware testbed for studying reliable agent execution over hours.

title: Mind Your Own Role: Reducing Role Overstepping for Effective and Efficient Multi-Agent Collaboration via Dynamic Role Activation Steering
summary: Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) have shown strong capability in solving complex tasks by assigning different agents specialized roles and corresponding subtasks. However, agents may overstep their assigned responsibilities and perform subtasks belonging to other roles, which can disrupt workflow, reduce system efficiency, and degrade task performance. To address this issue, we investigate role-related patterns in the model's internal activation space and uncover two key observations: (i) role instructions induce consistent directional shifts in activation space, and (ii) role-adherent and role-overstepping trajectories exhibit distinct activation patterns. Based on these observations, we propose Dynamic Role Activation Steering (DRAS), a lightweight and effective inference-time activation intervention approach to reduce role overstepping in multi-agent collaboration. Specifically, DRAS constructs a role steering vector and a lightweight role-overstepping detector for each role. During LLM generation, the detector estimates the probability of role overstepping from the current activation state, and DRAS dynamically adjusts the steering strength accordingly to guide the agent toward its assigned responsibilities. Experimental results show that DRAS effectively reduces the number of role-overstepping trajectories by up to 86.6% compared with Vanilla MAS, thereby improving task quality score by 10.0%--11.1%, achieving a 1.50$\times$--1.61$\times$ task-completion speedup, and reducing token consumption by 26.8%--38.7%.

title: Predict Before You Modify: Learning Improvement Dynamics for Self-Evolving Agents
summary: Self-evolving agents improve through repeated cycles of modification and evaluation. However, existing methods receive feedback on modifications only after costly evaluations, and aggregate scores may obscure distinctions between failures that require different repairs. We introduce predictive self-evolution through an editable Improvement Dynamics Model (IDM). Before evaluation, the IDM predicts task-level outcomes of a proposed modification and guides an optional revision. After evaluation, past modifications and their observed outcomes are used to improve the IDM, allowing predictive knowledge to accumulate across generations. The system can thus improve how it solves tasks, proposes modifications, and predicts their effects. Building on HyperAgents, we evaluate this approach across multilingual coding, paper review, robotics reward design, and Olympiad-level mathematical grading. Our approach outperforms HyperAgents across all four domains, with up to 46% higher average performance over generations. Gains also persist under matched token budgets that include both agent evolution and task evaluation, and extend to held-out tasks. Forecast accuracy improves as the IDM evolves, and the learned predictive knowledge transfers to improve evolution in a new domain.

title: VETNET: Assembling Benchmark Datasets for AI-Driven Veterinary Innovation
summary: VETNET represents an ecosystem of live benchmark datasets and evaluation frameworks designed to accelerate AI-driven innovation in animal science and veterinary medicine through standardized, high-quality datasets and multi-institutional collaboration across academic and non-academic sectors. This framework addresses the gap between AI advances in human medicine and the fragmented state of veterinary AI development.

title: RelLedger: Relational Information Governance for LLM Agent Organizations
summary: In LLM agent organizations, shared records determine which facts are available for later decisions. A sender consults interaction histories before deciding whether to report an event. A delivery gap across histories does not show whose relationship drove the choice or whether the resulting record matters downstream. We introduce RelLedger to audit these links. It holds the event, evidence, risk, and message fixed while crossing the sender's histories with the event target and an unrelated actor. Role reassignment and history rewrites locate the controlling cue. Message and cost interventions show when the effect appears. An attribution ledger maps each claim to its required response cells and separates missing interventions from sampling uncertainty. Recipient replay follows delivered information into downstream decisions. Executable workflows for a simulated one-person company extend the audit to retrieved histories, tool calls, and shared ledger updates. Across GPT, Gemini, Claude, DeepSeek, and Qwen, the audit reveals model-specific control paths and smaller relation gaps under explicit loss rules. Claude sends the same factual notice 62.22 percentage points more often with conflict histories than with friendly histories. In executable workflows, strained histories reduce recipient review rates by 45.83 points relative to warm histories for Claude.

title: Posterior Flow Matching
summary: Flow matching learns how to transport noise toward data, but its mean prediction does not directly report the endpoint uncertainty remaining at an intermediate state. This paper introduces Posterior Flow Matching (PFM), a general generative modeling framework that learns conditional velocity means and componentwise variances with a Gaussian posterior model. The same model evaluation supplies both a transport prediction and endpoint uncertainty, making posterior diagnostics available throughout generation. These learned moments support a mean-driven ordinary differential equation (ODE) and a posterior-driven stochastic differential equation (SDE), whose local noise scales adapt to the predicted uncertainty. Across image, point-cloud, molecular, and action generation, PFM improves generation quality and provides endpoint-posterior readouts throughout generation.

title: Unconstrained CTI-REALM with Open-Weights
summary: Organisations that want language-model agents for security work face a choice between open-weight models, which they can run and audit themselves, and far more expensive closed frontier models. We study that choice on CTI-REALM (arXiv:2603.13517), a benchmark in which an agent turns a threat-intelligence report into a working detection by querying a live telemetry store. We evaluate twenty-six models, nineteen open-weight and seven closed, under a common harness, scorer and panel of LLM judges. Our main finding is that an open-weight model can match the strongest closed models at less than a tenth of their cost, provided it is given enough turns. The benchmark's published limit on agent messages is a confound: a task that exhausts the limit scores zero on every checkpoint, including those it had already passed, so results at that limit partly measure which models finish in time. At the published limit the leading open-weight and closed models cannot be distinguished. With the limit relaxed, the models it was truncating recover, and the highest rewards belong to open-weight models. Among the leading models, price is a poor guide to capability: models with similar rewards differ in cost by more than an order of magnitude. Because the benchmark's checkpoint scores largely record what an agent did or mentioned, we also introduce stage-level metrics that score what the agent submits, by executing its detection queries in the telemetry store and judging its outputs against the answer key. Rather than combining them into one more overall reward, we show that different models lead different stages, which suggests routing each stage of the workflow to the model that performs it best rather than choosing a single model by its overall score. We also report how many tokens each model generates, and find that the share of output spent on thinking does not track the reward.

title: AgentCue: Statistical Summaries for Guiding Decentralized Multi-Agent Self-Organization
summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) combine multiple agents to solve complex tasks, and recent MAS scale to more than a thousand agents. At this scale, decentralized MAS remove the central orchestrator that assigns sub-tasks, and the agents, which we call workers, self-organize through their own choices of sub-tasks and collaborators on a shared board. As workers keep adding participation and collaboration records, however, the information explodes: workers spend more and more effort on reading the records of other workers, and self-organization loses efficiency. In the statistical view, we represent the execution history of an MAS by two continually updated networks, a collaboration network among workers and a participation network between workers and task types. We then propose AgentCue, a method built on a new latent space model that places workers and task types in a shared latent space. Each time the networks are updated, the estimated parameters of the latent space model form a compact and interpretable statistical summary, and workers use the statistical summary to choose sub-tasks and collaborators without repeated searches of the shared board. We establish the identifiability of the latent space model and non-asymptotic error bounds for the estimates under network increments, and we show that a fixed number of gradient updates after each network update suffices for the same error rate. Experiments on LongBench v2 Multi-Doc QA show that AgentCue achieves competitive effectiveness, efficiency, and interpretability.

title: GameSmith: Scaling Zero-Sum Self-Play with Synthesised Games
summary: Post-training large language models (LLMs) on two-player zero-sum games provides a verifiable reward, and the gains have been shown to transfer to general reasoning. Existing pipelines, however, rely on a handful of hand-written games and on advantage estimators tied to them, so both the supply of games and the advantage estimate on a large corpus limit scaling. We present GameSmith, which scales both. An LLM synthesises games inside templates whose reward, observation, and hidden-information code is fixed. Each game is verified by seed-paired replay and by an independent re-implementation of its specification, then expanded into encoding, rule, and size variants, giving 26 new games in 29 families and 336 verified variants from the three SPIRAL templates. The model is distilled from the self-play of a larger teacher (Qwen3-32B) on these games and then trained by self-play reinforcement learning with CRAB, an advantage estimator that credits each decision against a shrinkage estimate of the expected return of its position and is defined on every variant. On Qwen3-4B-Base, distillation raises the 13-benchmark mean pass@1 from 45.5 to 62.5, above the three SPIRAL games at the same budget, and self-play with CRAB reaches 64.9. The ordering holds across models, and transfer grows with the number of game families.

title: Visualizing the World Model in an Agent's Value Function
summary: Could model-free reinforcement learning algorithms actually be learning a model of the environment? In this work, we apply counterfactual interventions which hold everything about a state fixed, besides a targeted change, to explore if the value function of a Proximal Policy Optimization agent forms a world model of the Crafter environment. Despite only being trained to optimize reward, we discover that the value function learns concepts such as the rules governing when a diamond is collectible, water and food having an impact on health, heuristics regarding inventory, and more. Finally, we discuss the safety implications of our visualizations and some shortcomings of current reinforcement learning agents that will prevent us from building truly advanced machine intelligence.

title: DiTSG: Context-Aware Air Traffic Scene Generation with Multi-Agent Diffusion Transformers
summary: Understanding how many aircraft, and which traffic configurations, can be safely and efficiently managed by air traffic controllers within a given airspace is fundamental to air traffic management. Air traffic controllers continuously modify aircraft trajectories through interventions such as speed advisories and radar vectoring, and the patterns of these interventions are difficult to capture effectively using existing air traffic simulators. To address this limitation, we propose Diffusion Transformers for Traffic Scene Generation (DiTSG), which learns to generate air traffic scenes from recorded multi-aircraft trajectories. DiTSG employs stacked multi-agent inverted Transformer layers as the denoising backbone of a diffusion transformer, jointly generates the trajectories of multiple aircraft within a traffic scene, and conditions the generation on agent-specific required times of arrival. The resulting trajectories generated by DiTSG preserve realistic inter-aircraft interactions observed in actual air traffic operations. Experiments show that the DiTSG generates diverse traffic scenes that reproduce the statistical properties of recorded traffic while preserving realistic inter-aircraft interactions.

title: Splicing Hints into Reasoning Traces: Learning from Demonstrator Failures
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards improves mathematical reasoning when a final answer can be checked, but a correct answer does not certify the derivation behind it, and proof problems offer no answer to check. Replacing the check with a reasoning model as an in-loop verifier faces a fundamental obstacle: the policy must already produce occasional correct attempts for any reward to exist, which it may never do at olympiad level. We instead move verification and repair out of the training loop and into offline data generation with SPLICE, a workflow in which a second model, given only a reference solution, edits a reasoning model's traces as they are generated: it verifies progress, truncates a failed trace at its last verified step, and splices in an adaptively strengthened hint until progress resumes. The resulting dataset includes repaired examples whose sampled unaided trajectory failed, with failed continuations removed and progress repeatedly checked against the reference solution. A model finetuned on SPLICE traces outperforms the same model distilled from the reasoning model's unedited traces on AIME and, under a grading protocol validated against human grades, on olympiad proofs. The trained model's own traces show a corresponding behavioral signature: at difficult points it announces a branch in the style of the spliced hints and takes riskier steps, with predictive entropy rising there and just after, a pattern absent from the model trained on unedited traces.

title: Cross-Modal Latent Influence: Patch-Level Training Sample Attribution for Vision-Language Models
summary: Explaining a vision--language model (VLM) prediction requires tracing training-example influence to the multimodal evidence that mediates it, yet existing attribution methods largely operate only at the sample level. Recent latent-mediated influence methods provide feature-level attribution in language models, but lack the multimodal and spatial structure needed to ground influence in VLMs. We introduce MOSAIC (Multimodal Orthogonalized Sparse Autoencoders for Influence Characterization). It learns a shared sparse image--text latent space whose concepts are 1) sparse within each modality, 2) supported on contiguous image regions, 3) aligned to the phrases that describe them, and 4) approximately decorrelated. It then applies EK-FAC to decompose training-example influence through these concepts and localize their contributions to specific text phrases and image regions. We evaluate MOSAIC on Qwen and Gemma across captioning, chest X-ray understanding, and visual question answering. The learned features are more localized and coherent without degrading task behavior, and ablating influence-ranked latents changes model outputs more than ablating latents ranked by activation or frequency. We find that visual evidence can substantially reorganize training-data attribution while preserving more of the shared latent structure. MOSAIC thus connects where model behavior comes from with what multimodal evidence carries that influence.

title: Scaling Inference-Time Compute with Teams of Coding Agents
summary: Multi-agent systems promise a new axis for scaling inference: rather than having one agent think longer or sample more attempts, a task is split across many agents that work in parallel and coordinate. However, in practice, more agents can easily produce duplicate work, coordination failures, and higher costs. We therefore formulate team design as a compute allocation problem: starting from a solo agent, where should additional inference compute go to reach the reward-cost Pareto frontier? We build a minimal multi-agent harness from the ground up and trace this frontier by varying, one at a time, the workflow stage at which a lead delegates to its workers (planning, implementation, or verification), the models that form the team, and the number of workers. On ProgramBench, teams outperform solo agents but cost three to seven times as much. With the right compute allocation, however, a heterogeneous 17-agent team comes within 1.4 points of a strong homogeneous 5-agent team at 70% lower cost. This efficiency stems from three findings. First, planning is the most valuable use of workers: in a homogeneous team whose lead decides how many workers to spawn, a lead that delegates only planning to its workers, and then implements and verifies the code itself, matches the reward of a lead that delegates to workers throughout planning, implementation, and verification, at half the cost. Second, cheap models pay off as planners but not as implementers: a strong lead with cheap planners recovers 47.5% of the reward gain of an all-strong team for only 13.9% of its additional cost, whereas cheap implementers lower reward. Third, planners keep improving reward as the team grows, whereas implementers and verifiers plateau beyond four workers. Together, our results offer a guide to spending an agent budget where it counts, given the task, cost, and latency constraints a user has.

title: Enhanced Trading Systems with Intelligent Market Analysis
comment: 9 pages, 1 figure, 2 algorithms, 1 table. Accepted at ICAIA 2026 (proceedings pending)
summary: This paper proposes a hybrid reinforcement learning trading framework integrating intraday market data with transformer-based financial sentiment signals. The system extracts sentiment dynamics and semantic event clusters from financial news and incorporates them into a PPO-based trading agent. Experiments on intraday NSE data demonstrate improved risk-adjusted returns compared to price-only baselines.

title: Should SLMs be in the Driver's Seat? A Study of Local Models as Interpreters in Cloud-Written Agent Programs
comment: Accepted at SLM-Agents: 1st Workshop on SLMs for Agentic Systems, NeurIPS 2026
summary: The most accurate agents executing user-provided tasks are driven by large, cloud-hosted models, which solve them by reading the private data of the user. Agents powered by models small enough to run on edge devices keep that data local, but yield far worse results. A third option is to have cloud models write a program that devices execute: the data stays local, but as the program is written before any data is seen, it fails whenever a step depends on interpreting content that appears only at run time. We explore an intermediate architecture, in which the cloud-written program defers bounded questions over user data to a small local model through an ordinary function call. On AppWorld this improves the success rate of a code-only agent in all six combinations of backbone model and test partition we evaluate, by up to 14.9pp, recovering a substantial part of the gap to a cloud-hosted ReAct loop while keeping user data on the device.

title: Origin Attribution for Unsafe Behavior in Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Coding Systems
summary: As language-model-based coding agents evolve their programs and reuse code from one another, safety failures can acquire a history that extends beyond the agent in which they are detected. An unsafe change may originate in one agent, propagate through intermediate recipients, and survive subsequent revisions before an audit reveals it. Understanding this history is important for identifying the introducing change and distinguishing inherited behavior from independently occurring failures. We study origin attribution in self-evolving multi-agent coding systems: recovering the agent and program version that introduced an observed unsafe behavior into the target's code lineage, or determining that it arose locally. This task is challenging because rewriting obscures textual similarity, independent occurrences confound temporal ordering, and intermediate recipients can resemble the source. We propose a method that combines behavioral fingerprint matching with historical localization and recursive tracing. It compares candidate implementations beyond the unsafe outcome, retains evidence from multiple historical versions, and follows matching candidates upstream. On 158 queries across 85 controlled scenarios, the method achieves 96.8% exact attribution accuracy, compared with 77.2% for exhaustive fingerprint matching without recursion. Component ablations and evaluation on 34 additional queries using the same method and hyperparameters demonstrate the complementary roles of multiple representatives and recursive tracing. Further checks extend the evaluation to approval-boundary and resource-owner errors. Together, these results show how behavioral and historical evidence can recover the origins of unsafe behavior through code revision and cross-agent propagation.

title: SemTree: Judge-Aware Semantic Decision Trees for Inspectable and Repairable Rule Decisions
summary: Rule decisions such as content moderation, advertising compliance, and eligibility checks combine several conditions, exemptions, and missing-information cases, and an error can be fixed only once the failing condition is known. We introduce SemTree, a framework that represents a rule decision as a semantic decision tree: each node is a natural-language question with explicit Yes/No/Unknown criteria, a pluggable semantic judge answers it, and the branching structure is compiled on the answers that this judge actually gives. The executed path is the reasoning behind every decision, so errors are repaired where they occur: a reviewer corrects a single node and replays the rule, corrected nodes become training labels for the judge, and a tool-using LLM editor revises questions and subtrees while observing execution results. On all 8,276 ShARC test cases, a tree executed by a hosted judge reaches 67.70% accuracy with 2.99 questions per case, on par with asking the same judge for the final label (68.23%); an earlier tree compiled for a different judge scores 47.87% when executed by this judge, while a new tree compiled on this judge's answers to a 12-question initial pool already scores 64.39%. Node-level repair raises BANKING77 accuracy from 82.04% to 86.16%, an explicit exemption node cuts the false positives of a Chinese e-commerce moderation clause from 24 to 5, and a trained editor raises the development accuracy of edited trees from 64.47% to 73.35%.

title: Harness^2: Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World
summary: LLM agents' capabilities depend not only on their underlying models but also on their execution harnesses. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a promising approach to automatically evolve these harnesses. However, deploying RSI in open-world settings still faces two critical challenges. First, open-world tasks are typically unseen during the harness design phase and novel at test time, leaving no ground-truth verifiers to reliably guide online harness edits. Second, the RSI process remains highly task-specific and fails to generalize to novel scenarios. We introduce Harness^2, a plug-and-play, recursive agent harnessing framework that addresses these challenges through two connected levels of recursion. Task-level recursion refines the current task's harness using a contrastive Propose-Probe-Compose step that reliably guides edits without ground-truth verifiers, and can be scaled further via parallel or sequential recursion. Harnessing-level recursion then extracts experience from these edits to update a continual improvement harness, enabling the agent to better adapt to future tasks. Across three professional benchmarks and four model-harness configurations, a single step consistently improves GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash over their base harnesses, yielding gains of up to 11.5 points on WorkBuddy-Bench, 4.5 points on JobBench, and 11.8 percentage points on LAB, with further gains as the task-level recursion budget increases.

title: Degrees of Freedom in Multi-Agent Coordination: Between Centralized and Decentralized Regimes
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) are commonly organized around two coordination regimes. Centralized coordination provides explicit control but can create a bottleneck at a single coordination locus, whereas decentralized coordination offers local autonomy but must achieve effective collaboration through distributed decisions and experience. These trade-offs motivate a systematic study of the space between the two regimes. We introduce Degrees of Freedom (DoF), a continuous configuration framework that quantifies the size of the decision space delegated to downstream agents. DoF controls the granularity of delegated work and the target probability that each task unit is assigned to the branches. Its endpoints recover the two coordination regimes. Across multiple task domains, DoF reveals a hierarchy of organizational effects. Delegated granularity and within-regime routing produce structured but bounded profile reallocations, whereas task domain and retained experience are associated with stronger differences between the centralized- and decentralized-branch profiles. The resulting performance landscape is task-dependent: different domains favor different DoF configurations, while atomic-target conditions are more consistent across runs. In-domain retained experience brings the two branch profiles closer together. The same controlled sweep reveals a task-dependent coordination landscape: some domains exhibit higher-performing configurations, whereas others show flatter responses and no single configuration dominates across domains. In five of the six evaluated state, an intermediate DoF configuration achieves higher mean accuracy than both endpoints, demonstrating the value of exploring the coordination space between them. Together, these findings provide empirical guidance for studying and designing intermediate coordination regimes in LLM-based MAS.

title: VH-GPO: Verified Handoff for LLM Agent Reinforcement Learning
summary: Group-relative reinforcement learning methods such as GRPO train large language model (LLM) agents by comparing rollouts for the same task. When every trajectory in a group fails with the same reward, relative advantages collapse toward zero, leaving no useful learning signal. A frozen teacher can recover from a student-visited state, but letting it complete the task makes the recovered suffix entirely teacher-generated. We ask: after repairing a student failure, when should control return to the student? We propose outcome-verified teacher-student handoff, instantiated in Verified Handoff for Group Policy Optimization (VH-GPO). The teacher provides enough support to reach a state from which the student can succeed, then returns control so that successful experience is again student-generated. Given an environment-verified teacher recovery, VH-GPO selects the earliest independently confirmed handoff point found within a bounded search budget. With Qwen2.5-1.5B, VH-GPO increases success rates over GRPO from 59.38% to 94.79% on ALFWorld and from 71.62% to 77.34% on WebShop. Improvements also hold with the 7B student, for which additional teacher and student output tokens amount to 1.77% and 2.61% of regular student rollout output tokens on ALFWorld and WebShop, respectively. Ablation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the key components. These results support using verified teacher assistance to repair failures while reinforcing the student's ability to complete tasks independently.

title: Echo: Error-Compensated 4-Bit Tensor-Parallel Communication for LLM Training and Inference
summary: Tensor parallelism ends every layer with an all-reduce that sits between two dependent matrix multiplications, so its cost cannot be hidden and grows as compute outpaces interconnect bandwidth. Sending 4-bit instead of 16-bit values would cut this cost by nearly 4x, but the all-reduce must add the values it carries, and rounding the sum injects an error at every call. Model quality depends on how these errors accumulate over layers, yet existing methods treat each call on its own. We present Echo, a 4-bit all-reduce for training and inference that controls the accumulated error. Echo moves data in 4 bits and sums in high precision, so each value is quantized at most twice per call for any number of GPUs. The summation reveals each injected error, and Echo feeds it back into later calls, so old errors cancel instead of accumulating. We prove that the accumulated error stays bounded independently of depth. On A100 GPUs, Echo is 2.09x faster than the 16-bit NCCL all-reduce on 1 GB messages. It speeds up the time to first token by up to 1.16x and the training step by up to 1.09x on an idle interconnect, and by up to 1.44x and 1.38x as background traffic grows. It keeps the average accuracy over seven benchmarks within 0.4 points of 16-bit inference on Qwen3-8B. In 10B-token pretraining, its final loss is less than 0.9% above that of 16-bit training. Echo needs no FP8 or FP4 hardware.

title: Strategic Multi-Agent Resource Allocation via Statistical Contracts
summary: We study a class of strategic hypothesis testing problems in which a principal aims to allocate resources among competing agents who possess data or data-generating mechanisms that may be relevant to the principal's goals. Each agent can pay a participation cost to opt into a statistical contract, in which case they generate data from a private distribution and receive an allocation based on a predetermined (and publicly known) mechanism. Each agent is either "null" or "non-null" and the principal's goal is to design the contract to limit the allocation to the former while maximizing transactions with the latter. Using e-values, we define a "continuous-closure," a set of allocations which prevents null agents from profiting in expectation and provides post-hoc risk control for general loss functions under arbitrary dependence. When the loss is the fraction of resources allocated to null agents, the region admits polynomial-time linear optimization. We also give explicit, interpretable closed-form approximations, and we analyze participation from a non-null agent's perspective, giving conditions under which entry into the contract is profitable. Finally, we extend the framework to support online arrival of the agents, in which case the principal has to make irrevocable on-the-fly decisions, and provide a method which gives time-uniform error-control in this setting.

title: PreSO: Privileged Representation Isolation for On-Policy Self-Distillation
summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) uses a self-teacher conditioned on privileged information to turn the sparse outcome signal of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) into dense token-level supervision. Yet the teacher's advantage may depend on information unavailable to the student at inference, raising a central question: which privileged changes are worth distilling? We use cross-problem recurrence as an empirical cue for potentially reusable guidance. Comparing the representation shifts induced by full solutions and compact hints, we find that hint-induced shifts are more concentrated and directionally consistent across problems, and yield more sustained downstream gains despite revealing less information. Motivated by this association, we propose Privileged Representation Isolation for On-Policy Self-Distillation (PreSO). At the source, PreSO uses compact hints to limit the solution-specific detail entering the privileged shift. At the target, it estimates a leading low-rank subspace from shifts pooled across related problems, projects the privilege-induced correction onto this subspace, and adds it to the student's unprivileged representation to form the representation-level distillation target. The selected subspace serves as an operational proxy for recurring structure, rather than a guaranteed separation of transferable and instance-specific information. On five competition-level mathematics benchmarks, PreSO consistently outperforms strong baselines across Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B, improving average accuracy over the base model by 6.8, 9.0, and 10.0 points. Beyond peak accuracy, PreSO attains the highest final-checkpoint average at every model scale, with improvements that persist through the end of training.

title: Controllable Diverse Sampling through Pullback Directions
comment: Accepted at the DynaFront workshop at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Conditional diffusion models can generate high-quality images that align closely with a given prompt. However, samples generated from different random seeds may remain visually similar, limiting creative exploration. Existing approaches can increase variation, but often require additional optimization or sampling overhead, while stronger perturbations may introduce distortions that degrade image quality or prompt alignment. We propose a training-free method that leverages the local pullback geometry induced by the mapping from the conditioning-embedding space to the image space to identify directions of maximal output sensitivity. By steering different sampling trajectories along these directions, we encourage distinct generations while maintaining consistency with the conditioning signal. Experiments on MS-COCO and BrushNet show the efficacy of the method in improving diversity on prompt-conditioned image generation and inpainting.

title: On Symmetry for Characterizing Agent Heterogeneity in Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Understanding agent heterogeneity can inform the design of shared and agent-specific policy representations, however existing criteria provide no unified structural test. We study finite-horizon POSGs and define a type-compatible transformation as a policy-evaluation symmetry when complete policy evaluation commutes with it for every decentralized behavioral policy. Policy-evaluation symmetries form a group for which agent orbits define structural agent types. This classification does not depend on the particular policy chosen or the distribution of initial states. We prove that every componentwise environment automorphism is a policy-evaluation symmetry, but that the converse does not hold. Applying the framework to cooperative Dec-POMDPs shows that agents can belong to different structural types even when they share a common reward. For prescribed weighted reward aggregation, we derive an exact value identity and sufficient conditions for the resulting Dec-POMDP to inherit the policy-evaluation symmetries of the source POSG. Finally, we give sufficient conditions under which repeated model factorizations induce policy-evaluation symmetry, and show that preserving an optimal Boltzmann policy set neither implies nor follows from this symmetry in general.

title: Showing versus Doing: Teaching by Demonstration
comment: Published at NeurIPS 2016 (oral presentation). 12 pages, including supplementary materials
summary: People often learn from others' demonstrations, and inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) techniques have realized this capacity in machines. In contrast, teaching by demonstration has been less well studied computationally. Here, we develop a Bayesian model for teaching by demonstration. Stark differences arise when demonstrators are intentionally teaching (i.e. showing) a task versus simply performing (i.e. doing) a task. In two experiments, we show that human participants modify their teaching behavior consistent with the predictions of our model. Further, we show that even standard IRL algorithms benefit when learning from showing versus doing.

title: ConicFlow: constrained Inference-time optimal control for flow matching models
summary: We propose ConicFlow, which frames constrained sampling from a flow matching model at inference time as an optimal control problem that balances deviation from the pretrained trajectory against reward, subject to hard terminal constraints. We discretize this problem and adapt receding-horizon control, optimizing only a short window of the trajectory at each step for computational tractability. We address the resulting sequence of receding-horizon subproblems with a receding-horizon primal-dual algorithm. Its dual multipliers capture the difficulty of satisfying each constraint and are refined throughout sampling, steering generation toward feasible final samples. We further propose a terminal-estimate variant that avoids accumulating local truncation errors by evaluating the reward and constraints at the predicted terminal point rather than at the end of the current horizon. Under standard regularity assumptions, we establish finite-horizon guarantees on suboptimality. Under convex-affine structure, we derive a sharper bound that scales linearly with omitted horizon length, and we show that the terminal-estimate variant is provably tighter when the flow dynamics change slowly. Experiments in both low- and high-dimensional settings with a recent large-scale flow matching model show that ConicFlow achieves high reward and strong constraint satisfaction while deviating less from the pretrained flow than recent baselines.

title: Optimizing Team Behavior via Extremum-seeking Control in Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning
comment: Accepted for publication at the 65th IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC 2026), Hawaii, USA
summary: In cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), agents must learn to coordinate their actions to achieve shared objectives. A key indicator of effective coordination is behavioral diversity, i.e., the agents' potential to enact distinct yet complementary control policies given the same set of observations. Although behavioral diversity can enable role specialization and richer joint behaviors, its appropriate level is highly context- and task-dependent and often costly to tune. We propose Adaptive Diversity Control (ADiCo), a two-timescale framework that adapts behavioral diversity online during training. On a fast timescale, Diversity Control (DiCo) regulates system diversity toward a target value. On a slower timescale, an Extremum Seeking Controller (ESC) adjusts this target using only mean episodic returns, without requiring an explicit model or analytical gradient of the diversity-performance landscape. We evaluate ADiCo on six configurations across two cooperative MARL tasks, where it maintains task-appropriate diversity levels: low diversity when homogeneous policies are beneficial and higher diversity when heterogeneous policies are required. Through this adaptation, ADiCo matches or exceeds the mean performance of DiCo (best grid-searched diversity target) and Unconstrained DiCo (diversity allowed to emerge without target regulation). These results demonstrate that incorporating classical feedback control into MARL training enables effective coordination by providing a systematic alternative to task-specific manual selection of the diversity target.

title: Coding LLMs Can Be Harnessed to Learn Interpretable Models from Data
summary: Since compact, interpretable classifiers correspond to simple programs, it is natural to ask if LLM-based coding agents can be used to learn interpretable models from data. In this paper we present a simple harness that repeatedly prompts a coding LLM to produce the next rule in a rule set, given a sample of labeled examples. We show that this approach is competitive with, and often superior to, state-of-the-art rule-learning methods on tabular data, especially with small training sets, and wins by large margins on text, including against another LLM-based rule learner; that this approach outperforms standard harnesses, and that the approach immediately leads to new kinds of interpretable models, since coding agents are not restricted to search a highly restricted hypothesis space. In addition to the advances made in learning interpretable models, these results are of interest because they introduce a new class of coding benchmarks - construction of interpretable classifiers - which includes quantitative measurements of output quality (i.e., test-set error) and existing mature ``specialist coding algorithms'' (i.e., existing learning methods).

title: Which Metadata Matters for LLM Tool Selection in MCP? Evidence from Controlled Factor-Level Interventions
summary: In Model Context Protocol (MCP) systems, LLMs select tools from metadata rather than from their implementations. Names and descriptions summarize what a tool does, while the parameter schema specifies the fields a tool accepts and how they are organized. Our analysis of metadata for 367,174 MCP tools reveals substantial schema variation among functionally similar tools. Many of these tools share names and similar descriptions but expose different parameter schemas. This raises a key question: can parameter-schema differences influence tool selection before any call is made? We study this question through controlled metadata interventions across five LLMs and five tasks. Each comparison changes exactly one metadata factor (server name, tool name, description, or parameter schema) while keeping the others fixed. We balance tool positions and use conditional logistic regression to estimate position-adjusted effects. We find that: (1) parameter-schema changes produce the largest and most consistent selection shifts among the tested interventions. Models tend to favor separate top-level parameters over grouped or composite forms. (2) Descriptions that explain parameters also tend to increase selection, while name effects are weaker and less consistent. (3) Targeted comparisons show that schema effects depend on the specific parameter names and on how the request represents the same information. When only one schema satisfies an explicit request requirement, all five models select the compatible tool despite position preferences. These results show that parameter schemas influence not only how tools are called, but also whether they are selected. For MCP developers and evaluators, schema design and tool ordering can therefore affect which implementation is invoked even when functionality is unchanged.

title: CoEvoke: Evoking Multi-Agent Collaboration for Trajectory Collection
summary: Training multi-agent collaboration requires trajectories of checking, feedback, and repair, yet task-solving rollouts may end in immediate approval or repeat unsuccessful attempts without useful correction. We introduce CoEvoke, a cross-domain framework that evokes these interactions during trajectory collection. Controlled perturbations create recoverable difficulties, while restricted reference-based guidance directs investigation. The resulting dataset contains 4,567 reconstructable trajectories over 4,130 software-engineering and reasoning tasks, linking public interactions to evidence, decisions, and task-native outcomes. Separate experiments over 2,287 same-task pairs show feedback increases of 47.72-100 percentage points across seven perturbation groups; guidance has smaller, model-dependent effects. With identical training tasks, decision-record counts, and updates, perturbation-enriched judge training improves ACPBench-Hard success from 35.38% to 42.12% (+6.73 points). SWE verifier training gains 7.60-9.40 points over interface-matched untrained references. Workflow and post-training evaluations preserve task-solving topology with unperturbed inputs and no private-reference guidance. These results support designing collection conditions to obtain corrective supervision that improves collaborative decisions with frozen solving agents.

title: What Can Language Models Inherit from Solomonoff Induction? Limits, Attainable Properties, and What Served Conditionals Reveal
summary: A familiar line of reasoning runs as follows: language models are flexible approximators trained under a strictly proper loss, so scale brings them closer to Solomonoff induction, and their predictive success is evidence of that approach. We apply known results from algorithmic information theory, universal prediction and Bayesian consistency. In its uniform form the conclusion holds for no computable model: each has cheap environments it never learns, and every uniformly computable family of total predictors shares one on which each member fails beyond a horizon growing with its index, so ``closer'' can hold only pointwise, one environment at a time. Nor could the offered routes certify even that: finite evaluation cannot certify agreement on rarely reached contexts, perfect corpus fit selects the corpus law as prior, and asymptotic criteria cannot see the constants that carry Solomonoff's guarantee. Our lens is the Kraft inequality read for predictors. Every model has at most the same budget of predictive success, so Solomonoff's predictor, which leaves part of it unspent, differs from a language model not in having more of it but in where it spends it; on mutually singular families this is exact, and only full-mass Bayes mixtures reach the frontier. We then discuss what is inheritable, including in-context learning as amortised Bayesian inference; what survives within a context window; which Solomonoff-like properties a deployed system should have or avoid; and what served conditionals determine. A closing table states what common practices certify and what to report. Tests are developed in a companion paper.

title: Actionable Meta-Requirements for AI Robustness Auditing
summary: AI-enabled systems must remain dependable when the conditions under which they operate change (e.g., due to input perturbations, distribution shifts, or changes in external dependencies). This makes robustness auditing of such systems important for judging whether the available evidence is sufficient to support a defined robustness conclusion. However, designing an AI robustness auditing framework is challenging. A key unresolved issue is determining the requirements such a framework should support; these requirements have not yet been consolidated. We address this gap through meta-requirements: higher-order requirements specifying what a class of auditing frameworks should support. In design science research, literature and domain experts are common sources of meta-requirements; accordingly, we derive the initial set from literature and validate and refine it with practitioners. Our systematic literature review retained 74 of 2,890 records and derived 43 meta-requirements across 16 categories. We evaluated them with 128 practitioners, obtaining 5,504 ratings and 586 substantive comments. Overall, 81.20% of ratings indicated agreement or strong agreement. In particular, 41 of the 43 literature-derived meta-requirements were classified as strongly supported. Practitioner feedback refined the requirements and identified an additional requirement concerning external components and supply chain dependencies. The final set comprises 44 meta-requirements across 16 categories, of which 43 received quantitative validation. These meta-requirements can help organizations implement AI robustness auditing frameworks, assess existing frameworks for completeness, and refine them.

title: ANASSA: From High-Level Framework to Low-Level Architecture for Spatial Agentic AI
comment: 14 pages, 2 figures, 13 tables. Design Science Research (DSR) study
summary: Agentic AI systems operating over geospatial data require more than autonomous reasoning and tool use; they must also support explicit orchestration, spatial validation, governance, provenance, failure handling, and human decision authority. Prior work introduced ANASSA, an agentic AI orchestration framework for spatial intelligence that established high-level components and responsibility boundaries for governed agentic execution (arXiv:2609.14824).
